title: Organization-Level Actions Policies
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of organization-level actions policies and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to organization-level actions policies.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on organization-level actions policies. Organization Actions policies constrain which action sources and permissions repositories may use; workflow YAML complements but cannot replace administrator policy. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Organization-Level Actions Policies matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Organization Actions policies constrain which action sources and permissions repositories may use; workflow YAML complements but cannot replace administrator policy. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Controlling which actions can be used
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Approved action sources
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Workflow permissions policies
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

items.title: Third-party action restrictions
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Governance across repositories
items.text: Record ownership, approval boundaries, version/pin choices, permission policy, and release evidence so another maintainer can explain and audit the automation.

items.title: Policy enforcement responsibilities
items.text: For policy enforcement responsibilities, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
name: Least-privilege workflow baseline
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Use only organization-approved actions and tools"
content_blocks.expected_output: The workflow declares read-only repository access. Organization-level action policies must be configured by administrators separately.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Review the workflow permission block together with your organization’s Actions policy and approved-action list.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Do not assume repository YAML can override organization or enterprise policy.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to organization-level actions policies. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain organization-level actions policies, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Standardize workflow behavior across teams without hiding important security boundaries.

content.task: Apply organization-level actions policies to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Organization Actions policies constrain which action sources and permissions repositories may use; workflow YAML complements but cannot replace administrator policy.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Organization Actions policies constrain which action sources and permissions repositories may use; workflow YAML complements but cannot replace administrator policy. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.

Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery.
